unit.title: Why doing what is best for you can be worst for all
unit.needIt: Overfishing, traffic, price wars, dishes in a shared kitchen: each person does the sensible thing and everyone loses. Spotting the trap is how you get out of it.
unit.why: Two people want to work together to get a big reward. However, each person thinks they can get a bigger reward by cheating while the other person stays honest. Because both people think this way, they both cheat and end up with a much worse result than if they had just cooperated.
unit.outcome: Identify situations where individual choices lead to a bad group outcome.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you choose not to help with chores because you think someone else will do them. You also see it when everyone uses a public space until it becomes crowded and messy.
unit.do: Identify one thing you do daily that hurts your long-term goals. Create a small rule or 'penalty' to help you stay on track.

quiz.q: What does Glaucon say is the best outcome for an individual?
quiz.why: Glaucon describes the best outcome as doing injustice without paying the penalty.
quiz.quote: The best is to do injustice without paying the penalty.

quiz.q: What is the first law of nature according to Hobbes?
quiz.why: The first law of nature tells people to seek peace if there is a chance of obtaining it.
quiz.quote: So the first law of nature is a two-part law. It says, seek peace if there's a chance of obtaining peace, and if there is, not engage in war.

quiz.q: What is the second law of nature?
quiz.why: The second law of nature involves giving up rights only if others do the same.
quiz.quote: The second law of nature tells you to be willing to lay down your rights to the extent that others are willing to do the same, and to content yourself with as much liberty against others as they have against you.

quiz.q: What is the 'third choice' in the prisoner's dilemma?
quiz.why: The third choice is a state of total war where both parties are in a state of war.
quiz.quote: Or it can be the case that A behaves in a warlike fashion, whereas B behaves in a peace-like fashion. Now, what's important to notice about the structure of the prisoner's dilemma is that A has control over which row obtains.

quiz.q: What is an example of the tragedy of the commons?
quiz.why: The lecture uses industrial pollution as an example of the tragedy of the commons.
quiz.quote: Each of you did the thing that was rational, but the coordinated effect of your actions gave you a wildly suboptimal result, an environment full of pollution.

quiz.why: Tit-for-tat means cooperating in the first round and then following the lead of the co-player.
quiz.quote: So, for example, you might adopt a strategy of cooperating in the first round of a Prisoner's Dilemma game and then following the lead of whatever your co-player does in subsequent rounds of the game. That, as you know from your reading, is called a tit-for-tat strategy.
